title: $80,000 spent. Do you have to finish?
hook: Walking away feels like wasting what you spent. Does that money change the choice?

knows: that money already spent cannot be got back
how to add up costs and income
doesNotKnow: that only future costs and benefits can change which choice is better
that a sunk cost appears in every option and so cancels out

misconception: I have spent so much already, I must finish.
objective: The learner can explain that money already spent is lost whichever option is chosen, so it cannot make one option better than another; the decision depends only on future costs and benefits.

claims.text: With $80,000 already spent, stopping leaves you $80,000 down overall.
Finishing (costs $30,000, brings in $20,000) leaves you $90,000 down overall, $10,000 worse than stopping.
The gap between finishing and stopping is the same whatever amount was already spent.
claims.source: (−S − 30,000 + B) − (−S) = B − 30,000: the sunk amount S cancels.

claims.text: In this model finishing is better only when it brings in more than the $30,000 it costs.
The lesson is a simple model with dollars only, ignoring reputation, learning and other effects; it gives no advice about real projects.
claims.source: Framing of the lesson's own calculation in Demo.tsx. The sunk-cost principle: e.g. Mankiw, Principles of Economics, chapter 'Firms in Competitive Markets' (sunk costs).

recall.question: You paid $60 for a concert ticket (no refunds). On the night you feel ill and would enjoy staying home more. What should the $60 change about your choice?
options: Nothing: it is spent either way
Go only if the ticket cost over $50
recall.why: The $60 is gone whether you go or not, so it sits in both options and cancels. Only what you would enjoy from here on can decide.
